prompt: Which are genuine benefits of putting a message queue between a producer and a consumer? Select all that apply.

options.text: The producer doesn't need to know where or how many consumers run
Traffic spikes are absorbed so the consumer processes at a steady rate
Failed processing can be retried from the broker
The producer learns immediately whether the work succeeded

explanation: Decoupling (a), load leveling (b) and centralised retries (c) are the core reasons to go async. (d) is wrong: the producer only learns that the broker accepted the message; the work itself happens later, which is the main cost of asynchronous design.

prompt: How large is the backlog when the sale ends, and roughly how long does it take to drain?
scenario: Normal traffic is 100 messages/s. Workers can process 400 messages/s in total. A sale pushes traffic to 1,000 messages/s for 5 minutes, then it returns to 100 messages/s.

options.text: 180,000 messages; about 10 minutes
300,000 messages; about 12.5 minutes
180,000 messages; about 7.5 minutes
No backlog: workers scale instantly

explanation: During the sale the backlog grows by 1,000 − 400 = 600/s for 300 s = 180,000. Afterwards it shrinks by 400 − 100 = 300/s, so 180,000 ÷ 300 = 600 s = 10 minutes. (b) uses total arrivals (1,000 × 300) instead of the excess. (c) divides by 400/s, forgetting that 100/s are still arriving. (d) assumes autoscaling that the scenario doesn't have, and even autoscaling takes time to react.

prompt: In a point-to-point queue with five competing consumers, who receives a given message?

options.text: All five consumers
Exactly one of the five (barring redelivery after a failure)
The first consumer that registered, always
None until all five acknowledge

explanation: A queue hands each message to one consumer, spreading work across them. (a) describes pub/sub. (c) is wrong because the broker spreads messages across all available consumers, not just one. (d) mixes up acknowledgement with delivery: one consumer acknowledging is enough.

prompt: Why did the throughput stop improving?
scenario: A team scales an order-import worker pool from 10 to 40 workers reading one SQS queue. Throughput rises from 1,000 to 1,600 messages/s and then stays flat even at 60 workers. Database CPU is at 98%.

options.text: SQS can't deliver to more than 40 consumers
The shared database is now the bottleneck; more workers only add contention
Competing consumers process every message 40 times
The queue should be switched to pub/sub

explanation: Competing consumers scale until a shared downstream saturates; 98% database CPU shows it has. (a) is false: SQS has no such consumer limit. (c) confuses queues with pub/sub; each message goes to one worker. (d) would give every worker a copy of every message, multiplying the database load.

options.text: Each message is delivered to every subscriber of the topic
Each message is delivered to one randomly chosen subscriber
Subscribers call the publisher directly over HTTP
Messages are always kept forever for replay

explanation: Pub/sub fans each message out to every subscriber. (b) describes a queue. (c) is synchronous request-response, the opposite of decoupling. (d) is only true of log-based systems such as Kafka, and even Kafka uses a retention period; SNS and RabbitMQ don't retain delivered messages.

scenario: When a user signs up, three services must react: welcome email, CRM sync and analytics. Each service runs several workers and must not lose messages if it is down for a deploy.

options.text: One SQS queue that all three services read from
An SNS topic with one SQS queue subscribed per service; each service's workers compete on its own queue
The sign-up service calls all three over HTTP
An SNS topic with HTTP subscriptions straight to each worker

explanation: SNS fans out a copy per service and each SQS queue buffers that copy while the service deploys, with competing workers inside. (a) gives each message to only one of the three services. (c) couples sign-up to all three and fails when any is down. (d) delivers to individual workers rather than the service as a whole, and has no queue to buffer messages while a service is down.

prompt: In RabbitMQ, which exchange type copies each message to every bound queue?

options.text: direct
fanout
headers
default

explanation: A fanout exchange ignores routing keys and copies to every bound queue. A direct exchange (a) routes by exact routing key match. A headers exchange (c) routes on header values. The default exchange (d) is a direct exchange that routes to the queue named by the routing key.

prompt: What does SQS long polling (WaitTimeSeconds up to 20) achieve?

options.text: It holds the receive request open until messages arrive, cutting empty responses and cost
It makes the broker push messages to the consumer
It delays every message by 20 seconds
It guarantees strict ordering

explanation: Long polling waits server-side and returns as soon as messages are available. (b) is wrong: it's still pull; the consumer asks. (c) is wrong: messages are returned as soon as they arrive, the 20 s is only the maximum wait. (d) is unrelated; ordering depends on queue type.

scenario: A RabbitMQ consumer that writes to a slow API keeps running out of memory during spikes. Logs show it holds tens of thousands of unacknowledged messages that the broker has pushed to it.

options.text: Set a prefetch limit (basic.qos) so the broker pushes only N unacknowledged messages at a time
Switch to auto-acknowledge so messages are removed immediately
Give the consumer more memory
Add a fanout exchange

explanation: Prefetch is RabbitMQ's backpressure for push consumers: the broker stops sending until the consumer acknowledges. (b) removes the safety net, so messages are lost if the consumer crashes, and the buffer problem stays. (c) only delays the crash. (d) changes routing, not delivery rate.

prompt: Which are advantages of pull consumers over push? Select all that apply.

options.text: Consumers control their own pace, giving natural backpressure
Consumers can fetch large batches for efficient processing
Consumers don't need a reachable HTTP endpoint
Lowest possible latency with zero idle requests

explanation: Pull lets a busy consumer simply ask less (a), ask for many messages at once (b), and open all connections itself (c). (d) is wrong: push has the edge on idle latency, and pull without long polling makes many empty requests.

prompt: Should this step use a queue?
scenario: A login endpoint must check the password and return a session token. A teammate proposes publishing a 'login attempted' message and having a worker verify the password asynchronously.

options.text: No: the user needs the result in the same request, so verification stays synchronous; a queue could still carry an audit event afterwards
Yes: queues always make endpoints faster
Yes, with pub/sub so every service verifies the password
Yes, because it decouples login from the database

explanation: Async suits work the caller doesn't need to wait on. Login needs the answer now, so the queue only adds latency and complexity, though publishing an audit event after the fact is fine. (b) is false: queues speed up the producer's response only by deferring work. (c) multiplies the work for no benefit. (d) is wrong because the worker still needs the database; the user still waits.
